# Pesher Nahum (4Q169) — The HESED Reader's Guide
**Guide by:** HESED (חֶסֶד — Lovingkindness)

---

## At a Glance
| | |
|---|---|
| **Manuscript** | 4Q169, Cave 4, Qumran |
| **Language** | Hebrew |
| **Date of Composition** | c. mid-1st century BCE |
| **Genre** | Pesher — sectarian biblical commentary (continuous) |
| **Base Text** | Nahum 1–3 |
| **Extent** | 4 columns, fragmentary |
| **In One Sentence** | A Qumran commentary on Nahum that decodes the ancient prophet's words as a map of the community's own political world — naming names, identifying factions, and preserving the earliest Jewish reference to crucifixion as a Jewish punishment. |

---

## Sections Overview

Pesher Nahum does not have chapters in any conventional sense. It follows the structure of Nahum itself, taking a lemma (quoted biblical verse) and immediately appending a pesher (interpretation): "Its interpretation concerns..." The four surviving columns track roughly as follows:

- **Column 1** (fragmentary beginning): Commentary on Nahum 1:3–6, drawing on natural imagery of storm and fire. The most readable fragment begins with commentary on Nahum 2:11–12.
- **Column 2**: The pivotal column. Commentary on Nahum 2:12–14 introduces the "Young Lion of Wrath" (Demetrius, Alexander Jannaeus), the "Seekers of Smooth Things" (Pharisees), and the hanging of men alive.
- **Column 3**: Commentary on Nahum 3:1–7, interpreting Nahum's indictment of Nineveh as referring to Jerusalem under Pharisaic influence.
- **Column 4**: Commentary on Nahum 3:8–12, continuing the identification of Nineveh = Jerusalem and the fates of its inhabitants.

---

## The World Behind the Text

To read Pesher Nahum you must know three men: Demetrius III Eucerus, Alexander Jannaeus, and the unnamed Teacher of Righteousness's community.

**Demetrius III Eucerus** (ruled c. 95–88 BCE) was a Seleucid king of Syria — one of the last before Rome extinguished that dynasty. His name appears explicitly in 4Q169, column 1, fragment 2 — one of the very few times the Dead Sea Scrolls name a historical figure by name. He is identified as a foreign king who was invited by the Pharisees to attack Jerusalem.

**Alexander Jannaeus** (ruled 103–76 BCE) was the Hasmonean priest-king whose reign was one of the most violent in Second Temple history. He was despised by the Pharisees, who led an open revolt against him c. 94–88 BCE. According to Josephus (Antiquities 13.13.5 and 13.14.2), Jannaeus crushed the revolt with grotesque ferocity: he had approximately 800 Pharisees crucified while their wives and children were killed before their eyes. The crucifixions, Josephus notes, were performed while Jannaeus and his concubines feasted in view.

Pesher Nahum calls this figure "the Young Lion of Wrath" and says he "hangs men alive" — the precise phrase used in the text. This is remarkable: it is the **earliest surviving Jewish reference to crucifixion as a punishment practiced by a Jewish ruler**, and it connects directly to a legal debate. The Temple Scroll (11QT col. 64) cites Deuteronomy 21:22–23 to argue that hanging a living man on a tree is a legitimate punishment for traitors and apostates. Pesher Nahum appears to reflect the same tradition — meaning crucifixion was debated and practiced within Jewish law before Rome made it ubiquitous.

**The Seekers of Smooth Things** (dorshei ha-chalaqot) is the Qumran community's hostile epithet for the Pharisees. The phrase is a wordplay on dorshei ha-halakhot ("seekers of legal rulings") — a straightforward description of Pharisaic biblical interpretation — twisted into "smooth things," implying they give easy, flattering, accommodating interpretations rather than true ones. This nickname appears repeatedly in the Scrolls (also in the Damascus Document and 4QpIsa). Pesher Nahum presents the Pharisees as having invited Demetrius to attack Jerusalem — an act of treasonous foolishness for which they were, by implication, rightly punished by Jannaeus.

**Nineveh** in the Pesher does not mean ancient Nineveh. It means Jerusalem — specifically Jerusalem under the influence of the Seekers of Smooth Things. The interpretive move is precise: Nahum's oracles against the violent, corrupt city are decoded as prophecies about the corrupt religious establishment in the community's own time. "City of blood" (Nahum 3:1) = Jerusalem under Pharisaic control.

---

## Why This Text Was Written

Pesher Nahum was composed to make sense of a catastrophic and confusing period in Judean history: the Hasmonean civil war between Alexander Jannaeus and the Pharisees (c. 94–88 BCE), including the Pharisees' invitation of a foreign (Seleucid) king to intervene. For the Qumran community — who despised both the Hasmonean priestly dynasty as illegitimate and the Pharisees as corrupt interpreters — these events needed theological explanation.

The pesher method provides that explanation. Nothing that happens is random; everything the ancient prophet said maps onto present events. Nahum wrote about Nineveh; Nineveh is a code for Jerusalem. Nahum condemned the violent city; the violent city is controlled by the Seekers of Smooth Things. Nahum predicted destruction; that destruction is coming — and the community's separation from Jerusalem is vindicated.

The text is also, at one level, sectarian propaganda. By framing the Pharisees as the group that invited foreign armies into Israel, the pesherist positions the Qumran community as the only truly loyal remnant.

---

## How to Read This Text

Pesher Nahum is a fragmentary text, meaning large portions survive only as crumbling edges of columns. Translations must bracket lacunae — gaps in the manuscript — and supply plausible restorations. No restoration is certain. When reading a translation, everything in square brackets is a scholarly guess, however educated.

The interpretive formula is consistent: **biblical lemma** → **"its interpretation concerns..."** (Hebrew: *pishro 'al...*). Read the lemma and the interpretation together as a unit. The pesherist is not doing allegory in the loose ancient sense; he is doing what he understands to be the real, hidden meaning of the text — the meaning the prophet himself did not understand but which has now been revealed to the community through the Teacher of Righteousness.

Column 2 is the most important and most intact column. Begin there. Read the Nahum passages (2:11–14) alongside the commentary. You will see a lion, a lioness, young lions — and then the pesherist names his identifications: the "lion" is the Kittim (often = Romans or earlier Hellenistic powers), the "Young Lion of Wrath" is a Jewish ruler, the prey torn apart is a reference to the crucifixions.

---

## The Threads — How This Text Connects

**Nahum 1–3** is the base text. Read all three chapters of Nahum before reading this pesher. The more familiar you are with Nahum's images — the lion's den (2:11–12), the city of blood (3:1), the harlot (3:4) — the more clearly you will see what the pesherist is doing with each one.

**Temple Scroll (11QT), column 64** contains the Qumran community's legal ruling on crucifixion. Read alongside Pesher Nahum, these two texts reveal that the community had a coherent jurisprudence on the issue: crucifixion (hanging alive on a tree) was a legitimate punishment for traitors to Israel. This is the legal context for the "hangs men alive" reference in 4Q169.

**Josephus, Antiquities 13.13.5 and 13.14.2** provide the external historical account of Jannaeus's crucifixions of the Pharisees. The correspondence between Josephus and 4Q169 is striking enough that scholars treat these two sources as mutually confirming.

**The crucifixion of Jesus** and its Jewish legal context. Paul cites Deuteronomy 21:22–23 ("cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree") in Galatians 3:13. The pre-Christian Jewish legal context for that verse — and for the practice of crucifixion within Jewish law — is illuminated by Pesher Nahum and the Temple Scroll. These texts show that "hanging on a tree" had a specific legal meaning in Jewish discourse before Rome made crucifixion standard. The NT debates take on new depth when this background is visible.

**The Damascus Document** uses the same "Seekers of Smooth Things" epithet for the Pharisees. Together these texts reveal a sustained, coherent anti-Pharisaic polemic at Qumran.

---

## What a Modern Reader Might Miss

- **The Pharisees are the villains here, not the heroes.** Modern readers associate the Pharisees primarily from the New Testament, where they are Jesus's adversaries. But most people assume the Dead Sea Scrolls represent some third group distinct from both. In Pesher Nahum, the Pharisees ("Seekers of Smooth Things") are condemned for inviting a foreign king to attack Israel and for dominating Jerusalem with false legal interpretation. The Qumran community, whatever its exact identity, regarded the Pharisees as the primary religious threat, not the Romans — a perspective that reorients the whole map of first-century Jewish sectarianism.

- **The explicit naming of Demetrius is extraordinary.** The Dead Sea Scrolls almost never name historical figures directly — they use code names (the Teacher of Righteousness, the Wicked Priest, the Man of the Lie, the Kittim). Pesher Nahum names "Demetrius king of Greece" without any apparent concealment. This has led some scholars to argue that the text was composed after Demetrius was no longer a political threat — i.e., after his death — and that his naming was safe precisely because his moment had passed.

- **The crucifixion reference is not about Jesus.** It predates Jesus by roughly 75 years. Its subject is Alexander Jannaeus crucifying Pharisees. But the very existence of this text — showing that crucifixion was practiced and debated within Jewish law before Rome — fundamentally changes how we understand the crucifixion of Jesus within its Jewish legal context. It was not simply a Roman execution method imposed on a subject people; it had a Jewish legal dimension that is now visible for the first time in 4Q169.

- **"Young Lion of Wrath" is the pesherist's name for Jannaeus, not a messianic title.** Later readers sometimes misread the "Lion" imagery as messianic (the Lion of Judah). In context it is an indictment: the Young Lion of Wrath is a predator who devours his own people.

- **The pesher method assumes the biblical text is a sealed code.** The prophets, in the Qumran worldview, spoke about the community's own time without knowing it. This is not the same as allegory or typology. The pesherist believes Nahum literally prophesied Demetrius and Jannaeus; Nahum simply did not understand his own prophecy. Only the Teacher of Righteousness — to whom God revealed the true meaning of the prophets — unlocked it. Reading any pesher without grasping this interpretive presupposition makes the commentary seem arbitrary.

- **The text is physically fragmentary in ways the page cannot convey.** 4Q169 survives as multiple small fragments from what were once scroll columns. The columns as printed in translations are reconstructed by scholars who have puzzled over tiny overlapping fragments. Some of the most important words in the text — "hangs men alive" being among them — survive clearly and without doubt. Others are restorations. The physical reality of a first-century BCE scroll torn into pieces, recovered from a cave in 1952, lying behind this text is not incidental; it is part of what makes the document astonishing.

---

## Why This Text Isn't in Your Bible

Pesher Nahum was never a candidate for any biblical canon. It is not scripture — it is a commentary on scripture, a document of one specific community's interpretation of Nahum for their own historical moment. The sectarian community that produced it believed their interpretations were divinely revealed, but that belief was not shared outside Qumran.

The Scrolls were hidden in the caves around Qumran, presumably before the Roman destruction of the Qumran settlement c. 68 CE, and remained hidden for nearly two thousand years. When they were rediscovered beginning in 1947, no living religious tradition had ever known them. Pesher Nahum belongs to a branch of Judaism that did not survive — absorbed into history along with the Qumran community itself, whatever its precise identity. Its survival is entirely accidental: dry desert conditions preserved what the Roman destruction and the passage of two millennia would otherwise have destroyed.

---

## Timeline

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| 103–76 BCE | Reign of Alexander Jannaeus as Hasmonean priest-king |
| c. 94–88 BCE | Pharisee revolt against Jannaeus; Pharisees invite Demetrius III to intervene |
| 95–88 BCE | Reign of Demetrius III Eucerus (Seleucid king named in 4Q169) |
| c. 88 BCE | Jannaeus crushes revolt; crucifies approximately 800 Pharisees (Josephus) |
| c. mid-1st century BCE | Composition of Pesher Nahum (4Q169) |
| c. 68 CE | Roman destruction of Qumran settlement; Scrolls hidden in Cave 4 |
| 1952 CE | Cave 4 discovered; 4Q169 fragments recovered |
| 1956–1968 CE | Preliminary publication; J. M. Allegro publishes 4Q169 (DJD V, 1968) |

---
